summary.text: The Late Heavy Bombardment is a hypothesized spike in asteroid and comet impacts on the inner planets and their moons, thought to have happened about 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago.
The idea comes from Apollo Moon rocks whose impact-melt ages fall in a narrow window, suggesting that many lunar craters formed in that period.
Once widely accepted, it is now debated, partly because the cluster of ages could come from sampling debris scattered by one large impact.

facts.label: Worlds struck
facts.value: Mercury, Venus, Earth, the Moon and Mars

facts.label: Main evidence
facts.value: Ages of Apollo impact melt rocks

facts.label: Popular explanation
facts.value: The Nice model of giant-planet migration

items.prompt: One popular model says the giant planets shifted their orbits long ago. How would that lead to a bombardment of the inner planets?

options.label: Their pull dragged the Moon closer
They blocked sunlight from rocky worlds
They smashed into one another
They scattered asteroids and comets inward

items.explain: In the Nice model, migrating giant planets scattered objects from the asteroid belt or Kuiper belt into the paths of the terrestrial planets.

items.prompt: Apollo melt rocks cluster in age around 3.9 billion years. Critics say this cluster may mislead. Why?

options.label: Many could be debris of one huge impact
Moon rocks cannot be dated by isotopes
The rocks were contaminated on Earth
Sunlight melts lunar rocks every day

items.explain: Ejecta from the Imbrium impact should be present at all Apollo sites, so the cluster might reflect material from a single event rather than several.

items.prompt: Why are lunar meteorites a useful check on rocks collected by Apollo astronauts?

options.label: They are always older than Apollo rocks
They never contain any impact melt
They sample spots far from the landing sites
They show no signs of ever being hit

items.explain: Lunar meteorites are thought to sample the surface randomly, so some should come from regions far from the Apollo landing sites.

items.prompt: Before this hypothesis, why did geologists assume Earth stayed molten until about 3.8 billion years ago?

options.label: Volcanoes erupted nonstop until then
No older rocks had been found
Older fossils had all melted away
The Moon's tides kept it too hot

items.explain: That date appeared in many of the oldest rocks and acted as a cutoff, so with no older rocks found, Earth was assumed to have been molten before it.

items.prompt: Almost no lunar melt rocks older than about 4.1 billion years have been found. What explanation needs no cataclysm at all?

options.label: Later impacts reset their age clocks
They sank into the Moon's core
Astronauts chose not to collect them
The Moon did not exist before then

items.explain: Older melt rocks may have existed, but continuous cratering over 4 billion years could have reset their radiometric ages or crushed them too small to date.

items.prompt: Earth's oldest known rock is about 4.03 billion years old. Where can scientists hold rocks even older than that?

options.label: In deep ocean trenches
In fresh volcanic lava
In ancient glacier ice
In meteorites that fall to Earth

items.explain: Older rocks reach Earth as asteroid fragments that fall as meteorites.
